title: The seven signs of life, and the cases that break them
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers Cambridge Stage 3 Biology Units 3.1 'Living and non-living', 3.2 'Growth and nutrition' and 3.3 'Movement and reproduction', and NIOS Level A Lesson 4 'The Environment' (what environment means; physical and biological parts; plants and animals; natural and human-made non-living things). No textbook needed.
summary: Your child learns the seven life processes scientists use to decide whether something is alive (MRS GREN), then puts them on trial against tricky cases: fire, crystals, robots, sleeping seeds and viruses. Along the way they follow growth in stages, find out how plants make food from air, water and light, watch a seedling hunt for light, meet nests, eggs and seeds, and see cells for themselves. They find that no single sign is enough, that the line between alive and not-alive is still argued about, and that living and non-living things are woven together into one environment.
builds_on: Class 1: alive, once alive and never alive; seeds sleep; yeast is tiny life. This rung adds the seven life processes, cells, growth, nutrition, movement and reproduction, the environment, and the hard cases. Later: microorganisms (Class 5), how life began (Classes 3 and 5), genes and inheriting features, and the web of life.
goals: By the end your child can name and explain the seven life processes (movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition).
By the end your child can test each sign against a tricky case and show why one sign alone isn't enough.
By the end your child can describe growth in stages for a human and a plant, and say how plants and animals get their food.
By the end your child can explain that living things are made of cells and pass on instructions to their young.
By the end your child can sort their surroundings into physical and biological parts, and natural and human-made things, and show how they depend on each other.
By the end your child can explain why scientists still disagree about whether viruses are alive.
words: how living things get energy from food, usually using oxygen
noticing and responding to the world
how green plants make sugar from light, air and water
alive but resting, like a dry seed
the tiny building block every living thing is made of
an instruction, passed from parent to young, inside every cell
everything around us, living and non-living

days.title: Mrs Gren and the seven signs
days.goal: Remember Class 1 and learn the seven life processes.

steps.title: Remember
steps.do: Ask: 'What's alive, once alive and never alive in this room?' Then: 'Remember the seed that slept for 2,000 years? Was it alive while it slept?' (Yes, dormant.) 'So how do you know something is alive?' Write every idea on a big sheet.

steps.title: Mrs Gren
steps.do: Teach the seven life processes with the memory name MRS GREN: Movement, Respiration (getting energy from food, using air), Sensitivity (noticing and responding), Growth, Reproduction (making young), Excretion (getting rid of waste), Nutrition (getting food). For each, your child acts it out and finds it in a human, a dog and a tulsi plant. Tricky ones for plants: they move slowly (leaves turn to the light, a touch-me-not folds), they take in air through tiny holes in their leaves, they get rid of waste gases and water and drop old leaves. Ask: 'Does a living thing have to do all seven at every moment?' (No: a sleeping seed does almost none, until it wakes.)

steps.title: Story: Is Fire Alive?
steps.do: Read the story aloud (Story tab). Ask the questions. Don't settle the answer; that's this week's job. Write 'Is fire alive?' at the top of the big sheet.

days.title: Put the signs on trial
days.goal: Test each sign on tricky cases.

steps.title: Guilty or not?
steps.do: Say: 'Today we're judges. Each sign of life is on trial. Is it good enough on its own to prove something is alive?'

steps.title: Crystal garden
steps.do: Start Experiment e1: grow salt or sugar crystals on a string. Ask: 'Crystals grow. Will that make them alive?' Your child writes a prediction.

steps.title: Set up the light box
steps.do: Set up Experiment e3: a shoebox with a hole in one end, and a cup of moong seedlings inside. Ask: 'Plants can't walk. Can they move?'

steps.title: The trials
steps.do: For each sign, your child finds something non-living that shows it. Moving: a car, a river. Growing: a crystal, a snowball, a city. Feeding: fire 'eats' wood. Respiration: fire needs oxygen. Making more: fire's sparks start new fires. Waste: fire makes smoke and ash. Sensing: an automatic door senses you. Then: a robot dog moves, senses and needs 'food' (charging). Ask: 'So is any one sign enough?' (No.) 'How many signs would you want before you said yes?'

prep.task: Sprout a cup of moong seeds in soil so you have 2–3 cm seedlings
Boil water for the crystal solution

days.title: Cells: what living things are made of
days.goal: See cells and learn the deeper test.

steps.title: Building blocks
steps.do: Show a brick wall or a Lego model. Ask: 'What is it made of?' (Small blocks.) 'What do you think living things are made of?' Peek at the crystal string: anything yet?

steps.title: Onion skin cells
steps.do: Do Experiment e2: peel the thin skin from inside an onion layer and look at it with a strong hand lens or a phone camera zoomed in through a magnifying glass. If you have a toy microscope, even better. Your child draws the pattern.

steps.title: The deeper test
steps.do: Say: 'Every living thing we know is made of cells. You are made of about 30 trillion. And when a living thing makes young, it passes on a set of instructions (genes) inside its cells, so a mango seed grows into a mango tree, not a cat. Over very many generations the instructions slowly change, and that is how new kinds of living things come about.' Ask: 'Does a fire pass on instructions? Does a crystal?' Then talk about voice v1, van Leeuwenhoek and his tiny animals, and ask its question.

need: a strong hand lens, or a phone and a magnifying glass, or a toy microscope
a drop of water, a piece of clear plastic

days.title: Growth and nutrition
days.goal: Explore growth in stages and how living things get food.

steps.title: Crystal and light-box check
steps.do: Look at the crystal string. Has it grown? Ask: 'Does it grow the way a plant grows, from inside, using food? Or does it just stick more salt on the outside?' (Crystals grow only by adding on the outside; living things grow from within, by turning food into new cells.) Peek quickly into the light box and close it.

steps.title: Growth in stages
steps.do: Lay out family photos (or draw): baby, toddler, child, teenager, adult, old person. Your child puts them in order and says the stage they are at. Then draw the plant's stages in a circle: seed, germinating seed, seedling, young plant, flowering plant, fruit with new seeds. Ask: 'Why is it a circle?' (The adult makes seeds, and they start again.) Say: 'That circle is called a life cycle.'

steps.title: What do they eat?
steps.do: Do Activity a1: a food survey of living things around the house. Explain photosynthesis first: 'Green plants make their own food, a sugar, from sunlight, the air (carbon dioxide) and water, in their green leaves, and they give out oxygen.' Then sort: makes its own food (plants), eats plants (cow, goat), eats animals (spider, lizard), eats both (crow, human), eats dead things (mushrooms, earthworms, some bacteria). Ask: 'What would happen if nothing ate dead things?' (Dead leaves and bodies would pile up forever; nothing would turn back into soil.)

steps.title: Alive Detective card game
steps.do: Play the card game (g1): each card is a mystery thing with clues; players decide alive, not alive or argued, and give a reason.

days.title: Movement and reproduction
days.goal: See how plants and animals move and make young.

steps.title: Light-box results
steps.do: Open the light box from Experiment e3. The seedlings have bent towards the hole. Ask: 'How did they move without legs?' (By growing more on the shady side, so they bend towards light. They sensed the light: sensitivity!) Compare animals: they move their whole body to find food, escape and find mates. Then talk about voice v4, J.C. Bose, and ask its question.

steps.title: Eggs, seeds and babies
steps.do: Say: 'Every kind of living thing reproduces, or it would die out.' Sort examples aloud: seeds (mango, rajma, dandelion), eggs (hen, crocodile, butterfly, frog spawn), live young (cow, human, dog). Then shelters: the baya weaver weaves a hanging grass nest; a tailorbird stitches leaves together; a sparrow tucks a nest behind an AC unit; a crocodile mother guards her nest and carries her hatchlings to the water in her mouth; a spider wraps her eggs in a silk sac. Ask: 'Why do some animals lay hundreds of eggs and others have just one baby?' (Lots of eggs, little care, many get eaten; one baby, lots of care.) Seeds are a plant's young, travelling to new homes by wind, water and animals.

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Your child does Worksheet ws1 (core) on the seven signs, growth, food, movement and young. Check it together; for each slip, ask 'Which life process is that? What's your evidence?'

days.title: Viruses: the great argument
days.goal: Meet the hardest case and the scientists who disagree.

steps.title: What is a virus?
steps.do: Explain: 'A virus is far smaller than a cell. On its own it does nothing: it doesn't eat, breathe or grow. But when it gets inside a living cell, it takes over the cell's machinery and makes thousands of copies of itself. Colds and flu are caused by viruses.' Then add a tardigrade: 'This tiny animal can dry up for years, doing nothing at all, then wake when wet.' Ask: 'Which is more alive, a dried tardigrade or a virus?'

steps.title: The debate
steps.do: Talk about voice v2, the giant viruses. Then run a real debate: your child argues 'alive' for 3 minutes, then 'not alive' for 3 minutes, then decides. Write both lists on the big sheet.

steps.title: NASA's definition
steps.do: Talk about voice v3: NASA needed a definition of life to know what to look for on Mars. Read it slowly: 'a self-sustaining chemical system capable of Darwinian evolution', and explain: something that keeps itself going using energy and materials around it, and whose young can change slowly over many generations. Ask: 'Does fire pass that test? Does a virus? Does a sleeping seed?'

days.title: One environment, living and non-living
days.goal: See how living and non-living things depend on each other.

steps.title: Environment map
steps.do: Do Activity a2 in a park, a garden or a lane: your child maps one small patch (2 big steps square). Label everything as biological (living: grass, ants, a tree, a bird, moss) or physical (non-living: soil, stones, water, air, sunlight, warmth, a wall). Then draw arrows: what does each living thing need from the non-living things? (Plants need sunlight, water, air, soil; ants need soil for their nest.)

steps.title: Natural or human-made?
steps.do: Say: 'Non-living things can be natural, made by nature (a river, a stone, the Moon), or human-made (a dam, a bus, a road).' Ask: 'Who made the river? Who made the dam?' Then your child does Worksheet ws2 (stretch). Ask about the tricky one: 'Is a brick natural or human-made?' (Made by people, from natural clay.)

steps.title: The atoms that travel
steps.do: Say: 'The water in your body was once rain, and before that sea, and maybe once inside a dinosaur. The carbon in you was once in the air, then in a plant, then in your food.' Ask: 'Could the soil be the same with no living things?' (No: worms, fungi and dead leaves make it.) 'So where does non-living stop and living begin?'

days.title: Verdict and teach it back
days.goal: Decide the case of the fire, and teach the signs.

steps.title: The verdict
steps.do: Hold a mock court: 'The case of the fire.' Your child is the judge and gives a verdict using everything: the seven signs, cells, passing on instructions, NASA's definition. Accept any verdict with good reasons. Then your child does Worksheet ws3 (challenge), answering aloud while you scribe the long answers.

steps.title: Project: museum of tricky cases
steps.do: Finish the project: a poster or a tray museum of five tricky cases (fire, crystal, sleeping seed, robot, virus picture) with each one's 'signs it has' and 'signs it lacks', and a verdict.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child teaches MRS GREN to the family, explains why fire isn't alive (or why they think it is!), and says one way living and non-living things depend on each other. Ask the check questions.

sections.p: Match each life process to an example.
pairs: a sunflower turning to the sun
using air to get energy from food
a cat's ears turning to a sound

sections.p: Green plants make their food from…

sections.p: How does each make young?
A dry seed shows almost no signs of life. Why do we still say it is alive?

worksheets.title: Signs on trial, and the environment

sections.p: Each non-living thing shows one sign of life. Match them.
How is a crystal's growing different from a plant's?
opts: the crystal only adds on the outside; the plant turns food into new cells inside

sections.p: Physical (non-living) or biological (living) part of the environment?
Natural or human-made?
Everything around us, living and non-living, is called our ____.
Which statement is true?
opts: Soil is made with help from worms, fungi and dead leaves
Soil has nothing to do with living things

sections.p: A robot dog walks, barks when it sees you and needs charging. Which signs of life does it show? Which does it lack?
Pick one living thing in your environment map. What non-living things does it need, and how?
What can a virus do on its own, outside a cell?
NASA's working definition says life is a chemical system that keeps itself going and can…
Give one reason a virus might be alive and one reason it might not be. Then give your verdict, and say what evidence would change your mind.
Alive, not alive, or still argued about?
An animal or seed that is alive but resting, doing almost nothing, is called ____.
Which sign of life does fire truly lack?
If a robot was built that could build copies of itself, and the copies slowly changed, would it be alive? Why or why not?
Some people call a river a living being, and some courts have given rivers rights. Using the seven signs, is a river alive? Is that the only way to decide?

experiments.title: Crystal garden
experiments.question: Crystals grow. Does that make them alive?
steps: A grown-up pours hot water into the jar.
Stir in salt (or sugar) a spoon at a time until no more dissolves.
Hang the string from a pencil laid across the jar so it dips into the water.
Leave it somewhere still for several days and check daily.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will anything grow? Will it be alive?'
experiments.observe: Crystals forming on the string and getting bigger.
experiments.why: As water evaporates, the salt can't stay dissolved and its particles line up into crystals on the string. The crystal grows by adding on the outside. Living things grow from inside by turning food into new cells, and they pass on instructions; crystals don't.
experiments.safety: A grown-up handles the hot water.

experiments.title: Onion skin cells
experiments.question: What are living things made of?
need: a strong magnifier, phone camera or toy microscope
steps: Break an onion layer and peel off the very thin, see-through skin on the inside.
Lay it flat on clear plastic with a drop of water.
Look through the strongest magnifier you have, or zoom with a phone camera through a hand lens.
Draw what you see.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'What will the skin look like up close?'
experiments.observe: A pattern of tiny boxes, like bricks.
experiments.why: Those boxes are cells, the building blocks of every living thing. An onion skin is one layer of cells thick, which is why you can see them. You are made of about 30 trillion cells!

experiments.title: The seedling that hunts for light
experiments.question: Can a plant move? Can it sense light?
need: a cup of moong seedlings 2–3 cm tall
a second cup of seedlings, left in the room
steps: A grown-up cuts a hole about 3 cm wide in one short end of the shoebox.
Put a cup of seedlings at the far end inside, put the lid on, and stand the box with the hole facing a bright window.
Leave a second cup of seedlings in the open room as a comparison.
Water both the same amount every day, opening the box quickly and closing it again.
After 3 days, open the box and compare.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'What will the seedlings in the box do? Will they look like the ones outside?'
experiments.observe: The box seedlings bend sharply towards the hole and may be pale and long; the room seedlings lean only a little towards the window.
experiments.why: Plants move by growing. The tip of the shoot senses which side the light comes from, and a growth substance (auxin) builds up on the shaded side, making those cells grow longer, so the stem bends towards the light. Moving, sensing and growing are three of the seven life processes, all happening in one silent seedling.

activities.title: Who eats what?
steps: List six living things: a plant, a cow, a spider, a crow, a mushroom, a human.
For each, find out or guess what it eats.
Sort them: makes its own food, eats plants, eats animals, eats both, eats dead things.
Draw arrows from food to eater, and from the Sun to the plant.
Add one arrow from every eater back to the soil: what happens when they die?
activities.outcome: A food chart showing that every living thing needs nutrition, but gets it differently.

activities.title: Environment map
steps: Mark a square of ground with string, 2 big steps on each side.
Draw a map of everything in it.
Colour living (biological) things green and non-living (physical) things brown.
Draw arrows from each non-living thing to the living things that need it.
Write one thing the living things give back (shade, dead leaves for soil, holes that let rain in).
activities.outcome: A map showing that the living and non-living parts of an environment depend on each other.

project.title: Museum of tricky cases
steps: Choose five tricky cases: fire, a salt crystal, a seed, a robot, a virus (draw it).
For each, write the signs of life it has and the ones it lacks.
Add your verdict: alive, not alive, or 'scientists argue'.
Present it to the family and take questions.
project.outcome: A poster or tray museum and a confident explanation.

game.title: Alive Detective
rules: Shuffle the mystery cards and put them face down.
One player reads a card's clues aloud.
Everyone writes: alive, not alive, or argued.
Turn it over. Right with a good reason: 2 points. The 'argued' cards score for any well-argued answer.

cards.front: I grow, I need air, I eat wood, I make babies from sparks.
cards.back: fire: not alive (no cells, no inherited instructions)

cards.front: I grow bigger and bigger in salty water, in beautiful shapes.
I sleep for years in the dark and wake with water.
I am made of one cell. I swim in pond water.
I walk, talk and sense you. I run on batteries.
cards.back: a robot: not alive (argued for the future!)

cards.front: I do nothing on my own, but inside a cell I make thousands of copies of me.
I have no mouth but I eat dead leaves through threads in the soil.
I flow, I move rocks, I carve valleys.
cards.back: a river: not alive (but full of life)

cards.front: I was a tree. Now I'm a table.
I make my own food from sunlight and can live for 1,000 years.
I am a tiny animal that can dry up, survive space, and wake again.
I am a cloud. I grow, move, and make little clouds.
I live inside your gut and help you digest food.
I am a computer program that copies itself and changes.

big: Is fire alive? What about a virus?
If we found something on Mars, how would we know if it was alive?
Where does non-living end and living begin?
Could a robot ever be alive?
Is a river alive? Some countries say a river can have rights.

challenge.q: Textbooks often give a neat list of signs of life, as if the question were settled. Is it?
challenge.hint: No. Fire shows many signs and isn't alive; a sleeping seed shows almost none and is. Scientists still argue about viruses, and NASA's definition is a 'working' one. A list is a tool, not the truth.

challenge.q: 'Living things move, non-living things don't.' True?
challenge.hint: Rivers, wind and cars move. Trees hardly do. Movement alone tells you nothing.

challenge.q: We say humans are the most important living things. Says who?
challenge.hint: Without bacteria, fungi and plants, there would be no soil, no oxygen and no food. Without humans, the rest of life would carry on. Who depends on whom?

perspectives.view: About as many bacterial cells live in and on you as human cells. Many of them help you digest food and fight illness. Ask: are you one living thing, or a crowd?

perspectives.who: The Ganga, and the people who call it Mother
perspectives.view: For many people the Ganga is a living goddess. In 2017 an Indian court briefly declared the Ganga and Yamuna 'living entities' with legal rights (a higher court later set this aside). Ask: what changes if we treat a river as alive?

voices.idea: A cloth-seller with no university degree, he ground his own tiny lenses and was the first to see bacteria and other single-celled life, which he called 'animalcules', in pond water and in scrapings from his teeth.
voices.then: The Royal Society in London doubted him at first, then sent observers who confirmed what he saw.
voices.now: He is called the father of microbiology. Microbes are the most common living things on Earth.
voices.ask: Why might experts doubt someone without a degree? What finally convinced them?

voices.who: Didier Raoult and colleagues (2003), France, and their critics
voices.idea: They described the mimivirus, a 'giant virus' so big it was first mistaken for a bacterium, with far more genes than any virus known, including genes for jobs viruses aren't supposed to do. Some of them argued that giant viruses deserve their own branch on the tree of life.
voices.then: Many virologists disagreed: giant or not, these viruses still can't copy themselves without a host cell.
voices.now: There's no agreement. Some scientists say viruses are alive only inside a cell; others say they're not alive at all; others say the question is the wrong one.
voices.ask: Should the word 'alive' have a sharp edge, or can some things be 'partly alive'?

voices.idea: To know what to search for on other planets, a NASA group wrote a 'working definition' of life: a self-sustaining chemical system capable of Darwinian evolution.
voices.then: It became widely quoted. The scientist often credited with it, Gerald Joyce, has said it wasn't his alone and that nobody claimed it was the final answer.
voices.now: It's still used as a useful tool, and still criticised. There is no single agreed definition of life.
voices.ask: If you were building a robot to search for life on Mars, what would you tell it to look for?

voices.idea: Bose, a physicist in Kolkata, built very sensitive instruments, including the crescograph, which magnified a plant's growth thousands of times. He showed that plants respond to touch, light, heat, injury and poisons with tiny electrical signals, rather like animal nerves and muscles.
voices.then: Many scientists in Europe were doubtful, partly because his claims were bold, and some of his ideas about plants having nerves and feelings went further than his evidence.
voices.now: His measurements of plant responses and electrical signals are accepted, and plant electrical signalling is a busy field today. Whether plants 'feel' in any way like animals is still argued about.
voices.ask: Bose showed plants respond. Is responding the same as feeling? What evidence would help you decide?

story.title: Is Fire Alive?
text: On the night before Holi, the whole lane gathered around the bonfire. The men had piled up wood and dry branches and cow-dung cakes all week, and when the priest lit it, the fire leapt up so fast and so high that the children screamed and stepped back.
Zoya stood next to her Aaji, holding her hand, and watched the flames. Aaji had been a botanist before she retired, and she still couldn't walk past a plant without telling you its name.
"Aaji," said Zoya, "is fire alive?"
Aaji smiled the smile she kept for very good questions. "What do you think?"
Zoya had learned about the signs of life at school, Mrs Gren and her seven signs. She counted on her fingers.

"It moves," she said. The flames were dancing. "It breathes, because if you cover it, it goes out; it needs air. It eats, because it eats the wood. It grows, look how big it's got. It makes waste: smoke and ash. And it has babies!" A spark had flown out and landed on a heap of dry leaves, and a small new fire was starting. A man stamped it out. "That was its baby," said Zoya. "Six signs. It even senses things: when the wind blows, it leans away."
"Seven signs," said Aaji. "So it's alive?"
Zoya frowned. It didn't feel right. The fire didn't feel like the neem tree, or the goat tied by the temple, or the baby asleep on her aunty's shoulder.
"Then it's alive," she said, slowly. "But it isn't."
Aaji laughed. "Good," she said. "Now you're doing science. When the list says yes and your gut says no, one of them is wrong. Let's find out which."
They walked a little way from the heat, to the old mango tree at the end of the lane. Aaji picked up a fallen mango from the ground and broke it open, and showed Zoya the big seed in the middle.
"When this seed grows," Aaji said, "what will it become?"
"A mango tree."
"Not a coconut tree? Not a goat?"
Zoya giggled. "No! A mango tree."
"Why?"
Zoya thought. "Because it came from a mango tree. It's got mango-ness inside it."

"Exactly," said Aaji. "Inside every seed, inside every living cell, there's a set of instructions, passed down from parent to child, all the way back. Mango trees make mango trees. And very, very slowly, over thousands of generations, the instructions change a little, so that living things can become new kinds of living things. That's what life does. It remembers, and it changes."
She pointed back at the bonfire. "Now, the fire's baby. That little fire on the leaves. Was it a copy of its mother?"

Zoya thought about it. The little fire hadn't looked like the big fire at all. It was just fire, eating whatever it landed on. If it had landed on paper, it would have been a paper fire; on wood, a wood fire. It didn't have instructions. It didn't remember anything. Nothing was passed down.
"No," she said. "It doesn't remember. Every fire just starts again from nothing."
"So," said Aaji, "is fire alive?"
Zoya looked at the flames for a long time. "It's not alive," she said finally. "It just behaves a bit like it. It's like... a copycat."

Aaji squeezed her hand. "Some scientists would agree with you. And some would say the line between alive and not-alive is blurrier than we think. There are viruses that sit right on the line, and scientists still argue about them. Nobody has the final answer."
Zoya liked that. Nobody had the final answer. That meant there was still something left for her to find out.

The fire was burning lower now, and the people were singing. Zoya held the mango seed in her hand, warm from the bonfire, carrying its long, long memory of mango trees, all the way back to the very first one.
story.epiphany: The seven signs of life are a useful checklist, but fire passes most of them and isn't alive; the deeper mark of life is passing on inherited instructions (genes) that can slowly change over generations (evolution), which fire lacks. The turn is Zoya realising the little fire 'doesn't remember'. Underneath: a grandmother scientist, trusting both evidence and intuition, and the honest message that the question is still open.
ask: Which signs of life did the fire show?
Why did Zoya feel it wasn't alive?
What does the mango seed have that the fire doesn't?
What did Aaji mean when she said life 'remembers, and it changes'?
Why did Zoya like that nobody has the final answer?

ideas.more: Fire, crystals and robots each show some signs; sleeping seeds show almost none. Scientists use many signs together.

ideas.idea: Life passes on instructions that slowly change.
ideas.more: Every living thing is made of cells carrying instructions (genes) from its parents. Over many generations, those instructions change: that's evolution.

ideas.idea: Living and non-living are woven together.
ideas.more: Water, air, soil and sunlight make life possible, and living things make soil, oxygen and even rock (chalk and coral). Physical and biological parts together make one environment.

unknowns: Are viruses alive? Scientists are still divided.
How did the first living thing come from non-living chemicals? Nobody knows for sure; it's one of the biggest open questions in science.
If life exists on another planet, will it be made the same way as ours? We have only one example of life, ours, to go on.

books.author: Molly Bang and Penny Chisholm
books.why: How sunlight becomes life, told by the Sun. Penny Chisholm is an MIT scientist who discovered one of the most common living things on Earth, a tiny ocean microbe.

books.author: Nicola Davies
books.why: Beautiful introduction to the living things too small to see.

check.q: What are the seven life processes?
check.a: Movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition (MRS GREN).

check.q: Fire shows many signs. Why do scientists say it isn't alive?
check.a: It has no cells and doesn't pass on instructions; every fire starts from scratch.

check.q: How is a growing crystal different from a growing plant?
check.a: A crystal only adds on the outside; a plant grows from inside by turning food into new cells.

check.q: How do green plants get their food?
check.a: They make sugar from sunlight, air (carbon dioxide) and water in their leaves (photosynthesis).

check.q: How did the seedlings in the box move?
check.a: By growing more on the shady side, so they bent towards the light they sensed.

check.q: Name three ways living things make young.
Why do scientists argue about viruses?
check.a: They can't do anything alone, but inside a cell they copy themselves and pass on instructions.

check.q: Name a physical and a biological part of your environment that depend on each other.
check.a: e.g. a tree needs sunlight, water and soil; soil is made partly by worms and dead leaves.

subconcepts: no single sign is enough: fire, crystals and robots
cells: the building blocks of every living thing
inherited instructions (genes) that slowly change over generations
growth in stages: life cycles of humans and plants
living things grow from inside; crystals add on outside
nutrition: plants make food from light, air and water (photosynthesis); animals eat; decomposers recycle
movement: animals move about, plants move by growing (towards light)
reproduction: seeds, eggs and live young, and the shelters made for them
viruses: on the edge of life
the environment: physical and biological parts
living and non-living are woven together (matter cycles through both)
